caseno: Appeal from original decree No. 33 of 1967.
lawyer:
Mozammel Huq ----- For the appellant.
A. R. Yusuf with Akhtar Imam ----- For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
The Trustees of the Port of Chittagong ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Sadharan Bima Corporation and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
4. Defendant No. 3 contested the suit on the ground that the suit is not maintainable in law, that it is bad for want of proper and valid notice under section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act, that it is barred by limitation and that there is no cause of action against this defendant. It is their further case that 45 drums in question did not land from the vessel at all. It was denied that the suit consignments landed under nil/wrong mark to the care and custody of the jetty, as stated by the carriers. Nil/wrong marks are discharged solely at the risk of the carriers. The Out turn Report of the vessel has been issued to the Steamer Agent showing the consignments as landed short. Accordingly, Short landing Certificates have been issued to the clearing agent of proforma defendant No. 4 on the basis of the out-turn Report. 

 10. Mr Mozammel Huq has next submitted that the suit is barred by limitation. The ship arrived at Chittagong port on 5-10-63. The last date of discharge from the ship was 22-10-63. He refers to sub-section (2) of section SOB of the Chittagong Port Act which is as follows:- 

 Mr Mozammel Huq submits that as per subjection (2) of Section SOB quoted above limitation will run from 5 days after 22-10-63 i. e., from 27-10-63. Under section 109 (2) of the Chittagong Port Act, the plaintiff must fire the suit within six months next after the accrual of the right to sue, i e., within 27-4-74. As the present suit was filed on 29-8-64, it is barred by limitation, he submits. 

 13. Mr Mozammel Huq next submits that alternatively, if the date of issuance of Short-landing Certificates i.e., 16-1-64, is taken to be the starting point of limitation, still then the suit ought to have been filed on or within) 6-7-64. This submission, too, has no legs to stand, because a Short landing Certificate tends to show that the claimed goods did not land at all. This certificate gives a cause of action, against the crriers and a not against the Port Trust. 

 14. What, then, is the starting point of limitation in a suit against the Port Trust in a case like this, when neither the carrier nor its agent, neither the consignee nor its clearing agent and not even the Port Trust has any positive information and materials, at the time when the vessel last discharged its goods, that the claimed goods have landed into the care and custody of the Port Trust. 

 Before we advert to this question, we propose to deal with the next submission of Mr Mozammel Huq. He contends that section 109(2) of the Chittagong Port Act, 1914 has provided for a special period of limitation of six months after the accrual of the right to sue. Whatever be the starting point of the limitation 27-10-63 or 16-1-64, the suit must be filed with-in 6 months thereafter and not afterwards. 

 Reading the entire section 109 as a whole, Mr Mozammel Huq submits, section 109(2) pro-vides for a special period of limitation for any-thing purporting to be done under the Chittagong Port Act. He submits that the action or inaction of the Port Trust as a statutory bailee of the claimed goods, under section 50A of the Chittagong Port Act, read with sections 151, 152 and 161 of the Contract Act, is involved in this case. The plaintiff must file the suit within six months after the accrual of the right to sue and not afterwards. Mr Mozammel Huq submits that the plaintiff's "right to sue accrues co-extensively with the accrual of cause of action. The notice period of one month will not be added to the special period of limitation of six months, because notice is not a cause of action. The cause of action arises before the notice is served. That is why in section 109 (1), the notice-giver is required to state "the cause of suit. Mr Mozammel Huq rests his argument on the proposition that accrual of the right to sue is synonymous with accrual of cause of action. The plaintiff may file the suit even without notice. It is for the defendant to decide whether he will invoke the protection of section 109(1) or not. The defendant may even waive the requirement of notice. The provision of serving a notice is no fetter to the plaintiff's right to sue. He has the right to sue immediately when the cause of action accrues. 

 The aforequoted legislations, Mr AR Yusuf contends, makes it abundantly clear that a special period of limitation has been prescribed in each case for anything done or purported to be done under the said Act. The plaintiff has to file the suit within the stated special period after the accrual of the cause of action. He agrees with Mr. Mozammel Huq that the notice period in the afore-quoted legislations cannot be added to the special-period of limitation, because, he agrees, notice is not a cause of action. The cause of action accrues before the notice is given. 

 17. But what distinguishes section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act from the afore-quoted legislations is the special phraseology of sections 109(1) and 109(2). Unlike the afore-quoted legislations section 109 (1) provides that unless a notice under this subsection is proved, the Court shall dismiss the suit". Section 109(2) provides that the suit must be filed within six months next after accrual of the right to sue. In all the afore-quoted legislations, the suit has to be filed within a stated period of the accrual of the cause of action. Mr Yusuf argues that from the language employed in Section 109(1), it is apparent that the plaintiff's right to sue does not accrue at all until be has served a notice under section 109(1). His right to sue will accrue after the notice period of one month is over and he must file the suit within six months thereafter. Section 109, therefore, preserves the general law of limitation. 

 21. It appears, therefore, that in the context of the special features of section 109(1), "accrual of the right to sue" in section 109(2) cannot be co-extensive with "accrual of the cause of action". Plaintiff's right to sue has been positively obstructed by the provision of notice in section 109(1). He can file a suit without a notice only on the pain of a mandatory dismissal. The dismissal will be automatic; even if the defendant fails to plead absence of notice or even if the defendant waives the notice. Under these circumstances, plaintiff's liberty to file a suit is not a right to sue at all. His right to sue accrues only after the expiry of the notice period of one month. The word "next" in section 109(2) is a clear pointer to that direction. Section 109(2) in our view do not set out special period of limitation" for actions or purported actions under the Chittagong Port Act. 

 The general law of limitation is unaffected by section 109(2). It only gives the Port Trust a protection against unnoticed legations and section 109 (3) affords it an opportunity to tender sufficient amends within 6 months next after the accrual of the right to sue. The plaintiff, however, has to file the suit within 6 months after the notice period is over. 

 22. Mr Mozammel Huq has referred to an unreported decision of Division Bench of this Court, FA No. 232 of 1963, Tajor Rahman vs Trustees of the Port of Chittagong decided on 20-12-72 where it has been held that Chittagong Port Act is a special Act and a special period of limitation has been prescribed therein. We have gone through the judgment and we find that none of the arguments advanced in this case has been put forward in the said case speaking with respect we find the decision has preceded on the uncial lenged assumption that the Chittagong Port Act has prescribed a special period of limitation. The decision, therefore, can hardly be taken to be a precedent. 

 23. Mr Mozammel Huq submits next that if the general Law of limitation is held to be applicable, then Article 2 of the Limitation Act Applies in this case. Article 2 provides that for compensation for doing or omitting to do an act alleged to be in pursuance of any enactment in force for the time being (in the then Pakistan), the period of limitation, is ninety days and the starting point of limitation is the date when the act of omission takes place. The alleged loss of 45 drums, took place while the appellant was under a statutory obligation to perform the functions of a bailee. This function of the appellant is contained in section 50A of the Chittagong Port Act, read with sections 151, 152 and 161 of the Contract Act, Article 2, therefore, has full force and application to the facts and circumstances of the present case. The suit is clearly barred even under the general law of limitation, he contends. 

 24. We do not think this submission has any validity either. It has been held in the case of Mohamed Saadat vs Administrator, Corporation of City of Lahore, AIR 1945 Lah 324 (FB) that Article 2 is intended to afford protection to persons acting in pursuance of an enactment against state claims. A short period of limitation is provided for in such cases in order that such acts which are of public nature shall not give rise to protracted litigation. It has also been held in Punjab Cotton Press Co. vs Secretary of State, AIR 1924 Lah. 169 that in order to enable to take advantage of the shorter period of limitation prescribed by this article, he must allege and show that he had reasonable grounds for justifying his action under the particular enactment relied upon by him and not that he arbitrarily, asserted or thought so. He must have assumed to act in the honest exercise of a supposed statutory power. No such case has been set up by the appellant. On the other hand, the case of the appellant is that the cargo did not land at all. It appears to us that the present suit is a suit for compensation for breach of an implied contract which his to be governed by Article 115 of the Limitation Act. 

 25. There remains the question as to from when the period of limitation will start in a suit against the Port Trust when neither the carrier nor its agent neither the consignee nor its clearing agent and not even the Port authorities have any positive information and materials, at the time when the vessel last dis-charged its goods hat the claimed goods have landed into the care and custody of the Port Trust. 

 26. Mr AR Yusuf has referred to the decision in M/s Malik Hiram and Sons vs M/s Isthomian Lines Inc PLD 1965 (Karachi) 455, where it has been held that the period of limitation starts from the date when the plaintiff obtains a categorical information to the effect that the goods had been fully discharged at the Karachi Port Trust. 

 27. We find that there is good reason to accept the ratio decidendi of the said decision we are dealing with a situation where all the concerned parties are either unaware or uncertain whether the claimed goods have landed at all. It is only when the plaintiff is given definite information that the claimed goods have landed into the care and custody of the Port Trust, supported by document or documents that he is in a position to maintain an effective action against the Port Trust. The period of limitation will run from the date of that definite knowledge. From Exhibit 10(k) dated 20-11-64 we find that the defendant No. 2 wrote a letter to the plaintiff informing positively that the 45 drums landed in the jetty and enclosing therewith a copy of the Joint Inspection Report Exhibit A Before that date the defendant No. 2 is on record to have addressed a letter dated 18-5-64 to the clearing agent of proforma defendant No. 4 (Exhibit) passing on the same informal ion and claiming that they have in their possession documents to show full landing of the goods by marks or no marks, but that letter (Exhibit 1(g) cannot be said to be the starting point of limitation, because the knowledge transmitted to the plaintiff was unsupported by any documentation or evidence. Plaintiff's definite knowledge therefore dates from 20-11-64. Taking 20-11-64 to be the starting point of limitation we hold that the suit is clearly within time. 

 28. Mr AR Yusuf has submitted that the plaintiff filed the suit on 29-8-64 and ed there-in that they have already served a notice under section 109 and shall implead the Port Trust after expiry of the period of notice. In fact, he points out, the plaintiff issued the notice under section 109 on 8-1-65 (vide Exhibit 6) and the defendant No. 3 was impleaded as a party on 17-2-65. Taking 20-11-64 to be the starting period of limitation, the suit is still within time even if we hold that section 109(2) prescribes a special period of limitation of 6 months. But since we have already hold that section 109(2) does not prescribe a special period of limitation, we refrain from dealing with this submission of Mr AR Yusuf. We hold, however, that the starting point of limitation will be from 20-11-64 and that the suit will be governed by Article 115 of the Limitation Act.
